situation.note: my mother in law had a stroke and lives with us now. two kids, full time job, night care. I'm exhausted and nobody even notices. and I feel terrible for being angry at a sick woman.

understanding.bridge: What you are living with is what the texts call not feeling good enough, and that is where this week begins.
understanding.week_thesis: Seven days from carrying the weight alone to letting yourself be angry without becoming it, and finding one hour that is yours.

week_beats.hook: You recognise the exhaustion and the guilt, named without judgement.
week_beats.diagnose: You see that the guilt is what turns your anger into another weight, and that weight is what keeps you awake.
week_beats.steady: You hold that anger and guilt are both real, and that neither one is who you are.
week_beats.act: You try speaking the anger to one person, and you take one hour that is only yours.
week_beats.story: A woman who cared for a sick mother and her own children shows you how anger and love can live in the same heart.

understanding.core_struggle: A working mother of two who now also cares for her mother-in-law after a stroke; she is exhausted, unnoticed, and feels guilty for being angry at the woman she is caring for.
understanding.mirror: You give the day everything, and the night too, and then lie awake with a mind that will not settle.
understanding.insight: You are carrying three lives and nobody sees it. Underneath that is the guilt that makes you fight the anger, so you end up fighting yourself.

queries.hook: The weight of carrying everyone, and the guilt that comes from being angry at the person you are caring for, and the exhaustion that has no name. Someone I love is seriously ill.
queries.diagnose: When the mind turns against itself, anger at the one you care for becomes guilt, and the guilt becomes another weight you carry alone.
queries.steady: Praise and blame, gain and loss, pleasure and pain come and go; what is yours is to stand in the middle and not be shaken.
queries.act: Lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down; speak your anger gently to the one you are caring for, or to a friend, and let yourself be angry without becoming it.
queries.story: A woman who cared for a sick mother-in-law and her own children, who felt the anger she was not allowed to feel, and who learned to hold it without letting it become her.

verse.speaker: Arjuna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse.sanskrit: न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्याद्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम् । अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम् ॥
verse.line: Even winning everything wouldn't touch this grief that's drying me up inside.
verse.translation: I see nothing that could drive away this sorrow that is drying up my senses, not even an unrivalled, prosperous kingdom on earth or rule over the gods.
verse.why: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

matched.label: I'm burned out and running on empty

prasang.title: Krishna and Arjuna on Arjuna's faint-heartedness
prasang.summary: Krishna challenges Arjuna's despair. Arjuna admits he is confused about what is right, cannot tell which choice is better, and asks Krishna to teach him.
prasang.lesson: Admitting you don't know and asking for help is where clarity begins.

verse.meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that even winning the war or ruling a vast kingdom would not cure his grief. He says he is dried up inside, and nothing in sight can drive the sorrow away. He admits he does not know what to do. He asks Krishna to teach him what is right. The verse shows that admitting you do not know what to do, and asking for help, is where clarity begins.
verse.for_you: You are physically home but not present with your kids. You feel guilty for being angry at your mother-in-law. The texts call this not feeling good enough. You do not have to figure this out alone. You can ask for help.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment when you feel unseen and let it be.
verse.scene_line: You are on the battlefield of your own life, dried up inside, and asking for help.
asks: How do I stop feeling guilty for being angry?
Can I be angry without being bad?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse.sanskrit: ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते । सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते ॥
verse.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.
verse.why: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

prasang.title: The person of steady wisdom
prasang.summary: Arjuna asks how a steady person speaks, sits and walks. Krishna describes someone content within, unshaken by sorrow, master of the senses, and traces how dwelling on things leads to anger and ruin.
prasang.lesson: Steadiness is built by guarding attention; anger starts with what you dwell on.

verse.meaning: Krishna is telling Arjuna what happens inside a person who has lost their footing. A mind that keeps returning to what it lacks, to what was lost or what is unfair, begins to build a case against the world. That case feels like love or duty at first, but it hardens into wanting. When that wanting is blocked, the mind turns hot. Anger is not the first step. It is the last step of a mind that has been feeding on its own story for a long time.
verse.for_you: The anger you feel toward your mother-in-law is not the real problem. The real problem is the story you keep telling yourself about being enough for everyone, and how that story leaves no room for your own exhaustion.
verse.try_today: Notice the exact moment your mind starts building the case against yourself or the day.
verse.scene_line: You are walking through a day where your mind keeps returning to what is not fair.
asks: How do I stop the story from building itself?
Where does the wanting turn into anger for me?
What would it look like to guard my attention today?

verse.speaker: Teacher
verse.setting: Rules of conduct for a renunciant.
verse.sanskrit: नात्यर्थं सुखदुःखाभ्यां शरीरमुपतायेत् । स्तूयमानो न तुषेत निन्दितो न शपेत्परान् ॥
verse.line: Don't wear out your body chasing pleasure or fleeing pain. Praised, don't gloat; blamed, don't curse others.
verse.translation: Let him not torment the body too much for the sake of pleasure or pain. Praised, let him not gloat; blamed, let him not curse others.

matched.label: I'm burned out and running on empty

verse.meaning: A teacher is setting rules for a renunciant, telling them to live with steady balance. The teacher says do not wear out the body chasing pleasure or running from pain. When praised, do not swell with pride. When blamed, do not curse the one who blames you. The point is to let the body rest and the mind stay calm, no matter what praise or blame comes your way.
verse.for_you: You are praised for your care and blamed for your anger, and both are wearing you down. The teacher is not asking you to feel nothing.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you are praised or blamed, and let your body stay still in it.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own rules of conduct, and the teacher is telling you to let the body rest.
asks: How do I stop my body from wearing out when I am praised or blamed?
What does it mean to let my mind stay calm when I am angry?
How do I let my body rest when my days have no rest?

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse.sanskrit: जितात्मनः प्रशान्तस्य परमात्मा समाहितः । शीतोष्णसुखदुःखेषु तथा मानापमानयोः ॥
verse.line: Self-mastered and calm, you stay centred in heat and cold, pleasure and pain, praise and insult.
verse.translation: For one who has conquered himself and is at peace, the higher self stays steady in cold and heat, pleasure and pain, honour and dishonour.
verse.why: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.
verse.misuse: Staying steady under insult is not accepting mistreatment; you can stay calm and still speak up.

prasang.title: Lift yourself by yourself; marks of the realised
prasang.summary: Raise yourself by yourself; you are your own friend or enemy. The self-mastered person stays calm in heat and cold, praise and blame, and sees friend and foe alike.
prasang.lesson: You can be your own best friend or worst enemy; choose friend.

verse.for_you: You are holding anger and guilt at the same time, and both are real. You are not the anger, and you are not the guilt. You are the one who has to carry both. The steadiness is not about being perfect.
verse.try_today: Notice when the anger rises and name it as a feeling, not as who you are.
verse.scene_line: You are Arjuna on the field, holding a bow while the world throws praise and blame.
asks: How do I stop the guilt from swallowing the anger?
Can I be steady without pretending I am okay?
What does it mean to be my own best friend here?

verse.speaker: Vidula
verse.setting: Queen Vidula rouses her son, who lies defeated and despairing after losing his kingdom.
verse.sanskrit: माऽऽत्मानमवमन्यस्व मैनमल्पेन बीभरः / मनः कृत्वा सुकल्याणं मा भैस्त्वं प्रतिसंहर
verse.line: Don't think less of yourself or settle for little. Set your mind on something good, and stop fearing.
verse.translation: Do not hold yourself in contempt, and do not keep it going on too little. Set your mind on what is truly good; don't be afraid. Pull yourself together.
verse.why: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

prasang.title: Vidula rouses her defeated son
prasang.summary: Kunti sends Yudhishthira the old story of Queen Vidula, who finds her son lying defeated after losing his kingdom. She shames, then reasons, then encourages him until he rises and fights for it again.
prasang.story_hook: A prince lay in bed after losing everything, until his mother walked in and refused to let him stay there.
prasang.lesson: Past failure doesn't define you. Results are uncertain, but those who never try never succeed.

verse.meaning: Queen Vidula finds her son Sanjaya lying defeated on the ground, having lost his kingdom to his enemies. She sees him giving up and tells him not to think less of himself or settle for so little. She says to set his mind on something good and stop fearing. She urges him to pull himself together, because those who never try never succeed, and the outcome of any fight is never certain.
verse.for_you: You are lying on the ground too, but no one sees it. You feel guilty for your anger, but that is not contempt for yourself. Set your mind on what is truly good. Stop fearing that your anger makes you a bad person.
verse.try_today: Speak your anger to one person, and take one hour that is only yours.
verse.scene_line: You are in your own quiet room, lying defeated after losing your own kingdom.
asks: How do I set my mind on something good today?
How do I stop fearing my own anger?
How do I pull myself together without feeling worse?

verse.speaker: Narada
verse.setting: Narada to Shuka on troubles that affect many people at once.
verse.sanskrit: न जानपदिकं दुःखमेकः शोचितुमर्हति / अशोचन्प्रतिकुर्वीत यदि पश्येदुपक्रमम्
verse.line: Don't just grieve over a problem everyone faces. If you see a way to fix it, act.
verse.translation: No one should sit alone grieving over a trouble that has struck everyone. Instead of grieving, act to remedy it if you see a way.
verse.why: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

matched.label: Someone I love is seriously ill

prasang.title: Narada consoles Shuka
prasang.summary: The sage Narada visits the young Shuka and teaches him how to meet sorrow: brooding doubles pain, the mind is healed by understanding as the body by medicine, act if you can fix it, and contentment is the real wealth.
prasang.lesson: Brooding doesn't heal pain, it grows it. Care for the mind as you would the body.

verse.meaning: Narada comes to Shuka, who is sitting alone in grief. Narada tells him that sorrow shared or acted upon is lighter than sorrow kept to oneself. The sage says that no one should sit alone grieving over a trouble that has struck everyone. Instead of grieving, act to remedy it if you see a way.
verse.for_you: You sit in the same room as your mother-in-law and your children, yet you feel alone with the weight. The anger you carry is not a sign of failure. It is a signal that you have not let anyone else hold the load.
verse.try_today: Tell one person you are angry about the care load.
verse.scene_line: You sit with the stroke and the children, alone with the weight.
asks: How do I tell my anger from my care?

story.title: Queen Lila fears losing her husband
story.story_hook: Queen Lila was so happy with her husband that one night she was seized by the thought of losing him.
story.summary: Queen Lila loves her husband so much that she cannot bear the thought of his death. The wise tell her that nothing wins immortality, so she prays to the goddess Sarasvati instead. When the king dies, Sarasvati begins to show her that life and death are not what they seem.
story.lesson: Love brings the fear of loss; trying to control death only deepens the fear.

anchor.speaker: The brahmins
anchor.setting: Queen Lila, terrified of losing her husband, asks wise brahmins how to make him immortal.
anchor.sanskrit: तपोजपयमैर्देवि समस्ताः सिद्धसिद्धयः । संप्राप्यन्तेऽमरत्वं तु न कदाचन लभ्यते ॥
anchor.line: Discipline and prayer can achieve almost anything, but no one can win freedom from death.
anchor.translation: O queen, by austerity, prayer and discipline every kind of attainment can be reached; but immortality is never gained.
anchor.why: Love brings the fear of loss; trying to control death only deepens the fear.
anchor.misuse: Not fatalism about care: look after the sick fully. This is about the fear itself.

story.hook_title: Queen Lila was so happy that she became terrified of losing her husband
story.teaser: Queen Lila was so happy that she became terrified of losing her husband
story.for_you: You are caring for your mother-in-law and your children, and the weight of it is crushing. The anger you feel is not a betrayal of your care. It is the sound of a heart that knows it cannot hold everything together. You are not failing because you are tired.
asks: How do I hold my anger without becoming it?
